claims.text: The combination of high configurational entropy and nanoscale grain-boundary or interfacial barriers is the dominant factor preserving structural and chemical homogeneity in high-entropy nanoalloys.
High configurational entropy statistically stabilizes a random solid solution and opposes chemical segregation.
Random atomic distributions suppress phase segregation at moderate temperatures.
Nanoscale grain boundaries provide energy barriers that slow atomic diffusion.
A defective carbon support can stabilize ultrafine high-entropy nanoalloys produced by laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction.
Support interfaces create barriers to atomic rearrangement and thereby inhibit chemical separation.
High-energy nanoscale grain boundaries or support interactions arrest particle coarsening.
Laser-induced thermionic-emission reduction can produce uniformly distributed high-entropy nanoalloys with particle sizes below 10 nm.
The initial nanoalloys have random elemental occupancy and well-defined nanoscale grain boundaries.
Increasing heat-treatment temperature increases atomic mobility enough eventually to overcome entropy-related and interfacial stabilization.
Once the stabilizing barriers are overcome, clustering and phase separation occur.
The competition between stabilization and atomic mobility establishes a critical temperature below which the nanoalloy remains stable.
At a moderate treatment temperature such as 800 °C, the nanoalloy retains a uniform, single-phase microstructure and consistent elemental distribution.
Above the critical temperature, nanoalloys exhibit more clustering, secondary phases, or elemental inhomogeneity than the 800 °C baseline.
The prediction applies to nanoalloys with grain sizes below approximately 10 nm and exposures up to approximately 1100 °C.
For larger grains or substantially different support interactions, mechanisms other than configurational entropy and nanoscale interfacial barriers may dominate stability.
The critical temperature and the contribution of grain-boundary energy vary among high-entropy alloy systems and synthesis routes.
